title: UNIT 2: CHARACTERISTICS AND CLASSIFICATION OF ORGANISMS
notes:
✓ Living organisms have common characteristics such as cellular organization, metabolism, growth, reproduction, response to stimuli and adaptation.

Classification organizes organisms into groups based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

title: 2.1 Characteristics of Living Things
notes:
Living organisms generally show:
◆ Cellular organization → made of one or more cells.
◆ Nutrition → obtain materials and energy.
◆ Respiration/metabolism → release or use energy through chemical reactions.
◆ Growth → increase in size or cell number.
◆ Reproduction → produce new organisms.
◆ Excretion → remove metabolic wastes.
◆ Response → react to environmental stimuli.
◆ Movement → show movement of the whole organism or internal parts.
◆ Adaptation → possess features that help survival in an environment.

title: 2.2 Taxonomy of Living Things
notes:
✓ Taxonomy is the science of identifying, naming and classifying organisms.

It helps organize biological diversity by grouping organisms according to shared characteristics and relationships.

title: 2.2.1 Principles of Classification
notes:
Biological classification groups organisms using similarities and differences in characteristics.

Important criteria include:
◆ Cell type → prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
◆ Number of cells → unicellular or multicellular.
◆ Mode of nutrition.
◆ Cell structure and organization.
◆ Reproduction.
◆ Evolutionary relationships.

✓ Modern classification emphasizes common ancestry and evolutionary relationships.

title: 2.2.2 Taxonomic Hierarchies
notes:
✓ Taxonomic hierarchy arranges organisms from broad groups to specific groups.

Main ranks:
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.

MEMORY TIP:
King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

Species is the most specific major rank and consists of organisms with very similar characteristics that can generally reproduce naturally to produce fertile offspring.

title: 2.3 Relevance of Classification
notes:
Classification is important because it:
◆ Organizes the large diversity of organisms.
◆ Makes identification easier.
◆ Provides universal scientific names.
◆ Shows similarities and differences among organisms.
◆ Helps study evolutionary relationships.
◆ Facilitates communication among scientists.
◆ Helps predict characteristics of related organisms.

title: 2.4 Linnaean System of Nomenclature
notes:
✓ The Linnaean system uses binomial nomenclature, in which each species has two scientific names:

1. Genus → first name, capitalized.
2. Species epithet → second name, lowercase.

Example:
Homo sapiens.

Scientific names are usually written in italics or underlined when handwritten.

→ Binomial nomenclature provides a universal and standardized way of naming organisms.

title: 2.6 Five-Kingdom System of Classification
notes:
The five-kingdom system classifies organisms into:

1. Monera → prokaryotic organisms.
2. Protista → mainly unicellular eukaryotes.
3. Fungi → absorptive heterotrophs with chitinous cell walls.
4. Plantae → multicellular photosynthetic organisms.
5. Animalia → multicellular ingestive heterotrophs without cell walls.

title: 2.6.1 Kingdom Monera
notes:
✓ Monera includes prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria and cyanobacteria.

Characteristics:
◆ Usually unicellular.
◆ No true nucleus.
◆ No membrane-bound organelles.
◆ DNA is located in a nucleoid region.
◆ Reproduce mainly by binary fission.
◆ Nutrition may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.

Examples → bacteria and cyanobacteria.

title: 2.6.2 Kingdom Protista
notes:
✓ Protists are mainly unicellular eukaryotic organisms, although some are multicellular or colonial.

Characteristics:
◆ Have a true nucleus.
◆ Mostly aquatic or live in moist environments.
◆ Nutrition may be autotrophic, heterotrophic or both.
◆ Reproduction may be sexual or asexual.

Examples → Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena.

title: 2.6.3 Kingdom Fungi
notes:
✓ Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that obtain nutrients by absorption.

Characteristics:
◆ Mostly multicellular, except yeasts.
◆ Cell walls contain chitin.
◆ Do not photosynthesize.
◆ Body commonly consists of hyphae forming a mycelium.
◆ Reproduce by spores.
◆ Important decomposers.

Examples → mushrooms, molds and yeast.

title: 2.6.4 Kingdom Plantae
notes:
✓ Plantae consists mainly of multicellular eukaryotic plants.

Characteristics:
◆ Cell walls contain cellulose.
◆ Contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts.
◆ Mostly photosynthetic autotrophs.
◆ Store carbohydrates mainly as starch.
◆ Generally reproduce sexually and/or asexually.

Examples → mosses, ferns, flowering plants and conifers.

title: 2.6.5 Kingdom Animalia
notes:
✓ Animalia consists of multicellular eukaryotic animals.

Characteristics:
◆ No cell walls.
◆ Obtain food by ingestion.
◆ Usually capable of movement.
◆ Have specialized tissues and organs.
◆ Mostly reproduce sexually.

Examples → insects, fish, birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals.

title: 2.7 Renowned Taxonomists in Ethiopia
notes:
Taxonomic research in Ethiopia has been advanced by scientists and institutions involved in documenting the country's rich plant and animal diversity.

Their work includes:
◆ Identifying and describing Ethiopian species.
◆ Preparing biological collections and herbarium specimens.
◆ Studying endemic organisms.
◆ Documenting Ethiopia's biodiversity.
◆ Supporting conservation and scientific research.

title: UNIT 2 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
Characteristics of life → cellular organization, nutrition, metabolism, growth, reproduction, excretion, response, movement and adaptation.

Taxonomy → identification, naming and classification of organisms.

Hierarchy:
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.

Binomial nomenclature:
Genus + species epithet.
Example → Homo sapiens.

Five kingdoms:
◆ Monera → prokaryotic.
◆ Protista → mainly unicellular eukaryotic.
◆ Fungi → absorptive heterotrophs, chitin cell wall.
◆ Plantae → photosynthetic, cellulose cell wall.
◆ Animalia → ingestive heterotrophs, no cell wall.

EXAM TIP:

Eukaryote → true nucleus.
Fungi → chitin.
Plants → cellulose.
Animals → no cell wall.
